volumes.title: A Plank and Two Chairs
volumes.text:
The Bridge at Little Wend is a play for five players and any stage at all. You will need two chairs, set well apart, and a plank laid between them. That is the bridge. The left chair is the village of Upper Wend, the right chair is Nether Wend, and the floor is a cold brown stream.

Scene one. Dusk. Pim the tinker comes in pushing a handcart hung with pans. She stops at the bridge. Three planks are rotten through and the handrail has gone. On each bank stands a painted board, and each board faces the other village. Both say the same thing: MEND YOUR BRIDGE.

Pim reads one, walks round, reads the other. She tests a plank with her boot and it gives like wet bread. So she sits down on her cart, lights a stub of candle, and waits for somebody to come and explain.

volumes.title: The Widow’s Side
volumes.text:
Scene two of The Bridge at Little Wend. The stage is two chairs with a broken plank between them, and the left chair is the village of Upper Wend. Pim the tinker sits by her handcart in the last of the light.

Enter, from the left, the Widow Sorrel Agnew with a jar of honey and a look of long practice. The bridge belongs to Nether Wend. So does the mending of it, and so does the blame. Upper Wend has walked four miles round by the ford for forty years and can walk forty more. “All this over a bridge,” says Pim. “Over a kettle,” says the widow, and will say no more tonight.

She offers a bed in the bee-shed instead, which is warm and hums. The player should carry the candle off slowly, so that the far chair is left in the dark, listening.

volumes.title: The Miller’s Side
volumes.text:
Scene three of The Bridge at Little Wend. Morning. Two chairs and a broken plank; the right-hand chair is the village of Nether Wend, where the mill is.

Pim the tinker cannot cross the bridge, so she crosses the stream. The player takes off her boots, hangs them round her neck and walks under the plank. On a small stage this is the best joke in the play. Do not hurry it.

On the far bank Garrick Ould the miller is waiting, floury to the eyebrows, with his goat Bishop on a string. He has watched the whole crossing and offered no hand. The bridge, he says, is Upper Wend’s to mend. Upper Wend called his mother a thief over a copper kettle and has never said sorry. Then he notices the cart of pans across the water and asks, more quietly, whether she can fix a sieve.

volumes.title: Forty Years of Kettle
volumes.text:
Scene four of The Bridge at Little Wend. The two villages are two chairs, with a broken plank bridge between. Pim the tinker has spent a week mending pots on both banks.

Now the Widow Agnew sits in the left chair and Miller Ould in the right, both facing the audience. Pim stands in the stream between them. They tell her the story in turns, a sentence each, and it is very nearly the same story.

Forty years ago a copper kettle was lent across the bridge for a wedding breakfast. It never came back. The widow says the Oulds borrowed it and kept it. The miller says his mother sent it home and the Agnews hid it, for the pleasure of a grievance. After that nobody would mend a plank the other side might walk on. Pim asks who was married. Neither of them can remember.

volumes.title: One Nail
volumes.text:
Scene five of The Bridge at Little Wend. Two chairs are two quarrelling villages; the plank between them is a bridge nobody has mended in forty years. Early morning. Pim the tinker is alone with her handcart.

She has had enough of wading. She announces to the empty banks that she is not mending anybody’s bridge. She is laying one plank, only the one, so a cart can cross, and then she is going. She finds a board. She has a hammer. She has, after turning out every pan on the cart, no nails at all.

A boy has been watching from behind the left-hand chair. This is Jory, the widow’s grandson, nine years old and bound by oath never to help Nether Wend. He considers the matter. A tinker is not Nether Wend. He empties his pocket into her hand: eleven nails, borrowed from the bee-shed, still warm.

volumes.title: The Other Pocket
volumes.text:
Scene six of The Bridge at Little Wend. The stage is two chairs and a plank: two villages that do not speak, and their broken bridge. Pim the tinker and young Jory of Upper Wend have nailed down one board and run out of wood.

From behind the right-hand chair comes a plank, walking. Under it is Wren, the miller’s niece, who has dragged it from the mill woodpile and would like it known that she found it lying about. She is the same height as Jory. They have waved across the water all their lives and never once stood close enough to see the colour of each other’s eyes.

They meet in the middle of the bridge. Pim keeps hammering and pretends not to look. The children shake hands, very carefully, like ambassadors. Then Wren says, “You’re holding that nail wrong,” and the peace is properly begun.

volumes.title: Caught in the Middle
volumes.text:
Scene seven of The Bridge at Little Wend. Two chairs, two villages, forty years of quarrel; and on the plank between them Pim the tinker and two children, Jory and Wren, mending without leave.

The Widow Agnew enters left. Miller Ould enters right. They arrive at the same moment, which should look like an accident. Each orders the work stopped. Each then leans in to look at it. The widow says those are Agnew nails in an Ould plank. The miller says it is an Ould plank being ruined by Agnew nails.

Pim offers to pull the nails out again and leave everything as it was. Neither will allow it, since that would be giving something back. They are still arguing over how to un-mend a bridge when the sky rumbles. Behind the scenes, shake a sheet of tin. The children look up. The elders do not.

volumes.title: The Night the Wend Rose
volumes.text:
Scene eight of The Bridge at Little Wend. Night, and a storm. For rain, roll dried peas in a sieve; for thunder, shake a tin sheet. The two chairs are the villages of Upper and Nether Wend, the plank is their half-mended bridge, and the stream beneath is rising.

Miller Ould comes out with a lantern, calling for his goat. Bishop has slipped his string. A bleat answers from the middle of the bridge. The goat may be played by a horned head on a stick, or by a patient child. He has walked out as far as the new planks go and will not walk back.

The miller starts across and stops. On his side three boards are still missing, and the water is loud in the gap. He stands there with his lantern, and across the stream a second lantern comes out of the dark.

volumes.title: A Rope Across
volumes.text:
Scene nine of The Bridge at Little Wend. Storm. The plank between the two chairs is a half-mended bridge over a flooding stream, and in the middle of it stands the miller’s goat, Bishop, stuck. Miller Ould is on the right bank. On the left, with a lantern, is the Widow Agnew, his enemy of forty years.

She says nothing. She puts down the lantern, unwinds the rope she uses for hauling bee-skeps, and throws one end over the water. He catches it at the second try.

Widow and miller pull the rope taut between them for a handrail. The goat, given a rail to walk beside, strolls across as if it had been his own idea. He goes to the widow’s side and begins on her cabbages. She watches him eat a whole row and does not say a word.

volumes.title: What Was in the Loft
volumes.text:
Scene ten of The Bridge at Little Wend. The morning after the flood. Two chairs for two villages, a plank bridge between; we are at the right-hand chair, in Nether Wend, where the mill has had the stream through its ground floor.

Miller Ould and his niece Wren are carrying wet things up to the loft. A stepladder will do for the loft. Wren climbs, moves a row of meal sacks, and stops. She comes down with something round wrapped in a cloth. It is a copper kettle with a dent in one side.

Inside is a slip of paper in the hand of the miller’s mother. “Agnews’ kettle. To go back Tuesday, with thanks, and sorry for the dent.” The miller sits down on the bottom step. Forty years of Tuesdays have gone by. Pim the tinker, at the door, begins quietly polishing a pan.

volumes.title: The Kettle Goes Home
volumes.text:
Scene eleven of The Bridge at Little Wend. Two chairs are two villages that have not spoken for forty years, all over a borrowed kettle. The kettle has turned up in the miller’s own loft.

Miller Ould takes off his boots and wades across with it held high, as Pim the tinker did on her first morning. The Widow Agnew waits at the left-hand chair. He hands it over. She turns it round. “There’s a dent,” she says. “There’s a note about the dent,” says he, and gives her that too. She reads it twice, fills the kettle and sets it on to boil.

Now the bridge. The children, Jory and Wren, call for the last planks, and here the audience must help. The boards start at the back of the hall and are passed forward over every head, hand to hand, until they reach the stage.

volumes.title: Pim Crosses Over
volumes.text:
The last scene of The Bridge at Little Wend. The plank between the two chairs is whole. Upper Wend and Nether Wend stand one at each end of their bridge, and nobody quite likes to go first.

So Pim the tinker goes. She wheels her handcart over with every pan ringing, the first dry crossing in forty years. They ask her to stay, and she says pots do not mend themselves in other places. They ask her to name the bridge. She leaves that to the children, who have already decided. Jory and Wren hang up a new painted board, one board, facing the road: TUESDAY BRIDGE.

The widow pours tea from the copper kettle for the miller, the cast and, where the hall allows, the front row. Bishop the goat crosses twice more for the pleasure of it. Leave the plank in place until the audience has gone home.

volumes.title: The Stool Behind the Curtain
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the Corn Hall, first week of April. Opening night. I am Wynn Aldous, new prompter to the Hollow Lantern Company, and this is my diary of the season.

A prompter sits on a stool behind the left-hand curtain with the play open on her knee and one candle. When an actor loses a line she gives it, softly enough that the hall cannot hear and loudly enough that the actor can. Our play is The Salt Merchant’s Daughter. Our book has a marbled cover and Mrs. Quillfeather’s pencil in every margin.

Tonight I gave seven prompts: four to Tam Birdwhistle, who learns his part by hoping, two to Mrs. Quillfeather, and one to the carpenter, who has a single line. None to old Mr. Pell. He has played the Merchant for thirty years, and he looked at my stool as one looks at a spare umbrella.

volumes.title: The Causeway
volumes.text:
The marsh road to Reedham, mid-April. I am the prompter of the Hollow Lantern Company, and today I lost the end of the play.

Our wagon met a cart of reeds on the causeway, and Gooseberry, who is a horse of firm opinions, would not back up. The wagon tilted. One hamper, two masks and the prompt book went into the ditch. Barley Nock, our carpenter, fished them out with a rake. We dried the book page by page along a hawthorn hedge, like washing.

At dusk I counted the pages. The last one is gone: the Merchant’s closing speech and everything after it. I asked the company how the play ends. Mr. Pell said, “Grandly.” Mrs. Quillfeather said there was a ledger in it. Tam thought somebody forgave somebody. Nobody can give me the words, and we play Reedham tomorrow.

volumes.title: Nine Minutes of Salt
volumes.text:
Reedham, a barn, late April. I prompt for the Hollow Lantern Company, and since we lost the last page of our prompt book on the marsh road, the play has had no written ending.

Tonight Mr. Pell made one up. As the Salt Merchant he stepped forward and spoke for nine minutes by my watch. He covered the nobility of salt, the ingratitude of daughters, the price of herring, and a storm at sea that I am almost sure belongs to another play. The audience sat as people sit through weather. Then he forgave everybody and bowed.

I wrote down what I could catch in the back of the book, under the heading Ending, Reedham. Prompts given: five, none of them for the ending. A prompter cannot prompt what was never written. I sat on my stool with my mouth shut and felt like a lamp with no oil.

volumes.title: What Saltmere Wanted
volumes.text:
Saltmere on the Grey Coast, May. Wynn Aldous, prompter, Hollow Lantern Company. We are still playing The Salt Merchant’s Daughter without its last page, which went missing on the marsh road.

Mrs. Quillfeather had cut Mr. Pell’s new closing speech to two minutes. He took it bravely. But Saltmere is a town of fishing families, and when the Merchant began to decide his daughter’s future, a woman at the back called out, “Let the girl keep the boat!” Others agreed. A gull, which had come in through the net loft, appeared to agree as well.

Mrs. Quillfeather, as the Daughter, looked at the hall, looked at Mr. Pell, and said, “Father, I shall keep the boat.” It is not in any version. They cheered. I have written it in the margin with the date. Prompts: four, and one whisper to the gull, which did not take it.

volumes.title: Fog at Gullhaven
volumes.text:
Gullhaven, on the Grey Coast, late May. I am the Hollow Lantern Company’s prompter, keeping a book with its last page missing and its margins filling up.

The sea fog came into the hall with the audience and stayed. From my stool I could not see the far side of the stage, and Tam Birdwhistle could not hear me, so I gave his line twice, the second time rather loudly. A small girl in the front row repeated it for him, louder still. He thanked her as “madam” and went on. She prompted him three more times and was right twice.

The ending tonight kept the boat, kept two minutes of Mr. Pell, and gained a joke of Tam’s about a herring that I do not think can be stopped now. That makes three endings in the back of the book. Prompts: six of mine, four of hers.

volumes.title: Rehearsal in a Hayfield
volumes.text:
The fell road, Midsummer Day. Wynn Aldous, prompter to the Hollow Lantern Company, writing on an upturned bucket while the horse grazes.

We stopped in a hayfield to settle the ending of The Salt Merchant’s Daughter, the true one having been lost in April. I read out every version from my margins. Mr. Pell wants his speech back at full length. Tam wants the herring. Dorrie Finch, who keeps the wardrobe, wants whichever is shortest, because the Merchant’s coat is hot. They argued until the shadows moved.

Then Mrs. Quillfeather asked what I thought. Nobody has asked the prompter anything before. I said the best nights were the ones where the Merchant said least. Mr. Pell gave me a long look and then, to my surprise, a humbug from his pocket. We have agreed on nothing, but I am to keep writing down what happens.

volumes.title: Mr. Pell Dries
volumes.text:
Thistledown, in the Northern Fells, July. I am the prompter of the Hollow Lantern Company. We played tonight in a shearing shed that smelled of wool and held every soul for six miles.

Mr. Osric Pell has acted the Salt Merchant for thirty years and has never taken a prompt from anyone. Tonight, in the second act, in the middle of the scene with the ledger, he stopped. It was not a pause. I know his pauses. His hand went to his waistcoat, and his eyes went, very slightly, to the left-hand curtain.

I gave him the line: “And every grain of it accounted for.” He took it as if he had only been drawing breath, and the shed never knew. Afterwards he walked past my stool without a word and set a humbug on the open book. Prompts tonight: three. I have underlined one of them.

volumes.title: Rain at Cold Ashby
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, high in the Fells, August. Wynn Aldous, prompter, Hollow Lantern Company. The hall roof here is more of a suggestion.

It rained onto my stool all through the last act, and by the curtain the back pages of the prompt book had run blue. Those pages hold every ending we have tried since the true one was lost: Reedham, Saltmere, Gullhaven and the rest. I sat up by one candle at the inn and copied them out fair before they faded.

Copying is a kind of listening. Laid side by side, the endings grew shorter as the summer went on, and better. And I saw the one we have not dared. The Merchant says nothing at all. He looks at his daughter, closes the ledger, and puts it into her hands. I wrote that down too, small, at the foot of the page.

volumes.title: The Silent Ending
volumes.text:
Barleyford in the Lowlands, harvest fair, September. I prompt for the Hollow Lantern Company. Four hundred people came tonight, on benches, barrels and each other.

In the morning I showed Mrs. Quillfeather the ending I had written small at the foot of a page: no closing speech, only the Salt Merchant handing his ledger to his daughter. She read it and said, “Tonight.” Mr. Pell said he was being robbed of forty lines in his own lifetime. But he did it. He looked at her, shut the book, and held it out. She took it.

Four hundred people were quiet for as long as it takes to count ten. Then the benches came up like a wave. Mr. Pell stood in the noise with his hand on his heart, astonished. Coming off, he told me gruffly that we would keep it one more night, purely to be certain.

volumes.title: A Schoolmaster Remembers
volumes.text:
Mallow Green, in the Lowlands, late September. Wynn Aldous, prompter to the Hollow Lantern Company, on a quiet night: two prompts, both to Tam.

For a fortnight The Salt Merchant’s Daughter has ended in silence, with the Merchant handing over his ledger. The proper last page was lost in April and nobody misses it. After the play an old schoolmaster came round to the wagon. He had seen our piece thirty years ago, he said, and it did not end like that. There was a long speech, and a wedding.

Mr. Pell said there was certainly never a wedding. Mrs. Quillfeather said weddings need extra costumes. Dorrie Finch, of the wardrobe, said, “Over my hamper.” The schoolmaster went away shaking his head. But I lay awake. A prompter’s whole trade is the words as written, and I have spent a season helping to lose them.

volumes.title: Under the Wagon Seat
volumes.text:
The river road home, October. I am the prompter of the Hollow Lantern Company, and I have the missing page in my hand.

The wagon seat split this morning, and when Barley Nock lifted the board to mend it, there it lay: the last leaf of the prompt book, perfectly dry. It never went into the marsh ditch with the rest. It must have slipped down a crack when the wagon tipped in April, and it has ridden under us all season.

We read it aloud by lantern. The schoolmaster at Mallow Green was right. The Merchant speaks forty-one lines on duty and thrift, and then there is a wedding to a cousin nobody has met. Nobody said anything for a while. Then Mr. Pell cleared his throat. “I expect I was magnificent in it,” he said, “but I should not care to learn it again.”

volumes.title: The Last Night
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the Corn Hall, the last Saturday of October. Wynn Aldous, prompter to the Hollow Lantern Company, closing the book on the season.

We put it to a vote in the dressing room: the ending as first written, found last week under the wagon seat, or the one we made on the road. Five hands went up for ours, Mr. Pell’s first. So tonight the Daughter kept the boat, Tam had his herring, and the Salt Merchant gave up his ledger without a word. Emberwick stood. I gave no prompts at all, the whole evening, for the first time since April.

Afterwards I pasted the old page into the back, under the heading As First Written, and copied our ending fair at the front. Mrs. Quillfeather has asked me back for next year. Mr. Pell left a paper bag on my stool. Humbugs, a full quarter pound.

volumes.title: Two Hampers and a Trunk
volumes.text:
Emberwick, April, the week before the tour. I am Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper to the Hollow Lantern Company, and these are my notes, kept so that whoever has the hampers after me will know what is in them and why.

We have two wicker hampers and a tin trunk. They hold thirty-one costumes for five players, nine masks, a box of moustaches and one crown. Everything must fold, and everything must survive a wet wagon. A costume that cannot be sat on has no place in a touring company.

Mrs. Quillfeather wants a new gown for our last night in October, when she plays the Lady of the River. There is no money for cloth. So I shall beg one piece from every town we visit and see what a season makes. Mrs. Tansy the haberdasher has started me off: a yard of blue ribbon, the good sort.

volumes.title: The Fox’s Ear
volumes.text:
Reedham, in the marsh, April. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper, Hollow Lantern Company. Our wagon tipped on the causeway and the fox mask went into a ditch, so today’s notes are about the fox.

Our masks are paper and paste laid over a clay face, layer on layer, then painted. They weigh almost nothing. They also drink water like a hen. The fox came out with one ear folded flat and his whiskers, which are broom bristles, pointing every way. I have built the ear up again in strips, but in marsh air paste takes three days to dry. He hangs from the wagon hoop meanwhile, looking over the reeds with great interest.

A weaver here gave me half a yard of reed-green linen. It is for the River Lady’s gown, which I am piecing from one scrap out of every town on our tour. That makes two pieces.

volumes.title: A Coat with Seven Pockets
volumes.text:
Saltmere, on the Grey Coast, May. I keep the wardrobe for the Hollow Lantern Company, and the largest thing in it is Mr. Pell’s coat.

First, the gown I am making from one scrap begged in every town. A sailmaker on the quay has given me a square of old canvas, brown as strong tea. It will make the hem, where a river is muddiest.

Mr. Pell wears the coat as the Salt Merchant. It is plum velvet, older than I am, and I let the seams out a finger’s width every spring without either of us mentioning it. It has seven pockets. One is for his spectacles, one for humbugs, one for the letter he reads in the second act, one for a spare letter, and three he will not explain. An actor’s pockets are his own business. The wardrobe’s business is that nothing rattles.

volumes.title: A Ghost Made of Muslin
volumes.text:
Gullhaven, Grey Coast, late May. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper to the Hollow Lantern Company, with notes on the ghost.

Our ghost is eight yards of muslin hung from a willow hoop, with Tam Birdwhistle underneath holding the hoop above his head. In a dry hall it floats beautifully. In a Gullhaven sea fog the muslin took up the damp, hung like a wet sheet, and showed the audience a clear outline of Tam’s elbows. Then he trod on the hem. The ghost sat down. I am shortening it by a hand and sewing dried peas into the edge, so it swings clear of his feet.

For the River Lady’s gown, which I am making from a piece of every town we play, a netmender gave me a hank of fine twine. It will lace the back. That is four pieces now, and no one of them agrees with another.

volumes.title: Eleven Seconds
volumes.text:
The fell road, June. I am Dorrie Finch, who keeps the hampers for the Hollow Lantern Company. A farm we passed gave me a twist of grey wool for the gown I am piecing town by town, which makes five scraps. But today’s notes concern the quick change.

In our comedy Tam plays a farmer, the farmer’s aunt, a constable and a bishop, sometimes within the same minute. He changes behind a clothes-horse, with me. The rules are these. Hooks, never buttons. Each costume goes on over the last, like the skins of an onion. The hat is handed over last and put on while walking.

Our best time, farmer to aunt, is eleven seconds. Our worst produced a bishop in a bonnet. The audience at Gullhaven liked him so much that he has kept the bonnet in, and now I must find a spare.

volumes.title: The Crown and the Pie Tin
volumes.text:
Thistledown, Northern Fells, July. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper, Hollow Lantern Company. Notes on the crown, which is no more.

It was pasteboard covered in gold paper, and it had lasted six seasons. Last night the shearing-shed roof dripped on it for an hour. By morning it was a soft grey ring that would not have crowned a cabbage. We play the king tomorrow. So I borrowed a pie tin from the inn, cut points round the rim with the carpenter’s shears, bent them up and rubbed the whole with a rag. From the third row it looks finer than the old one. From the first row it says Thistledown Arms on the inside.

The innkeeper’s wife would not take the tin back. She gave me a horn button besides, for the River Lady’s gown that I am making from a scrap of every town. Six pieces, then, and a button.

volumes.title: The Moon Cracks
volumes.text:
Cold Ashby, in the Fells, August. I keep the wardrobe of the Hollow Lantern Company. The schoolmistress here has given a lace cuff for the gown I am piecing from every town, the seventh scrap. But today belongs to the Moon.

She is the oldest mask in the trunk, round and white with closed eyes, made before I was born by a wardrobe-keeper whose name is pencilled inside: A. Marrin. Last night the cold got into her. This morning there was a crack from the left eye to the chin. I laid a strip of linen along the back, pasted it, and held her by the inn fire until my arm ached.

The mend shows as a thin curved line beside the mouth. But it gives her the look of someone about to smile, and I am leaving it. Under A. Marrin I have pencilled: mended, D. Finch.

volumes.title: Washing Day at Barleyford
volumes.text:
Barleyford, in the Lowlands, September. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper to the Hollow Lantern Company. It is harvest weather, and thirty-one costumes have been worn in it.

So today everything that can be washed went into the river Ember, and everything that cannot was hung in the wind and spoken to firmly. Velvet is brushed, never wetted. Stockings are darned before washing, not after, or the holes travel. By noon the hedge behind the fairground was dressed as a king, a bishop, a ghost and a farmer’s aunt. A goat ate most of a ruff. I made a new one from a flour bag, and it sits better than the old.

For the River Lady’s gown, which I am building from one scrap of each town on our tour, a harvester’s wife plaited me a band of wheat straw, yellow as butter. Eight pieces. Soon I must stop collecting and start cutting.

volumes.title: Nothing Matches
volumes.text:
Mallow Green, in the Lowlands, September. I am Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper of the Hollow Lantern Company, and today I laid out the River Lady’s gown on a barn floor.

All season I have begged one scrap from every town: blue ribbon, reed-green linen, sailcloth, net twine, grey wool, a horn button, a lace cuff, a plait of straw, and from Mallow Green a strip of red flannel. Spread on the boards they looked like the inside of a magpie’s nest. I sat down among them and very nearly cried.

Barley Nock came in for a hammer and stood looking. He said the Ember does not match either. It is brown in the marsh, green under the willows and grey where it meets the sea, and nobody calls it a bad river. So I have laid the pieces in the order we travelled, hem to collar, and begun to cut.

volumes.title: The Villain’s Moustache
volumes.text:
The river road home, October. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper, Hollow Lantern Company. A short note on moustaches, written with a pricked thumb.

We keep six in a tin box. The best, the villain’s, is black horsehair knotted on gauze. The hair came from the tail of Gooseberry, our wagon horse, who has never forgiven it. A moustache is stuck on with gum, and gum does not care for soup. In the supper scene the villain’s moustache let go and swung like a gate while he threatened the heroine. He finished the speech holding it on with one finger, as if deep in thought. I have told him to do that every night.

The pricked thumb is from the River Lady’s gown, pieced from a scrap of every town on our tour. It is sewn as far as the waist. I work at it on the wagon, between ruts.

volumes.title: The Fitting
volumes.text:
An inn on the river road, October. I am Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper to the Hollow Lantern Company, and tonight Mrs. Quillfeather tried on the gown.

It is the River Lady’s, for our last night, and I have made it from a scrap begged in each town of the tour. She stood on a bench while I went round her with a mouthful of pins. The hem dips on the left. One sleeve is a thumb longer than the other. She touched the pieces one at a time and named them: Reedham, Saltmere, Gullhaven, the fell farm, all the way to the red flannel of Mallow Green.

Then she touched the front, where it gapes. It wants five fastenings and I have one horn button. The scrap bag is empty. I told her I would think of something, in the voice of a person who has not.

volumes.title: What the Gown Was Made Of
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the Corn Hall, the last Saturday of October. Dorrie Finch, wardrobe-keeper of the Hollow Lantern Company, with the last note of the season.

At noon the River Lady’s gown, made of one scrap from every town we played, still lacked four buttons. At one o’clock Mr. Pell knocked on the wardrobe door with a brass button off his own coat. Tam brought one of bone. Barley’s was wooden, whittled that morning. The prompter gave a small pearl one from her glove. With Thistledown’s horn button that makes five. I sewed them on in the order they came.

Mrs. Quillfeather wore it tonight. Under the lamps the patches ran together like water over stones, and the uneven hem looked meant. I have folded it into the trunk with a list pinned inside, saying where every piece came from. It lies next to the Moon, who appears to approve.

volumes.title: The Bill
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene is the parlour of the Sleeping Goose, an inn at Mallow Green: one table with a long cloth, one door, one window.

Mrs. Hobb, the landlady, has written out a bill for one week’s board. It is for Mr. Quince, the lodger in the back room, who has ink on his cuffs and nothing in his pockets. Hearing her on the stairs, he dives under the table. In comes a stranger in a black coat. Mr. Quince, certain this is a bailiff, answers his questions from beneath the cloth in the character of the table, and declares that no Quince has ever lived here.

The stranger is a piano tuner who has the wrong village. He leaves, shaken. Mrs. Hobb lifts the cloth and lays the bill on Mr. Quince’s knee. “No hurry,” she says. “I can count.” Curtain.

volumes.title: Mr. Quince’s Rich Uncle
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act, set in the parlour of the Sleeping Goose inn at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince, the lodger, now owes Mrs. Hobb for two weeks.

He announces that his wealthy uncle is arriving to settle everything. He goes out. A moment later the uncle comes in: Mr. Quince’s height, Mr. Quince’s boots, and a grey beard hooked over the ears. Mrs. Hobb is charmed. She would so like to see uncle and nephew together. So Mr. Quince runs out as one and in as the other, faster and faster, changing hats in the passage, until he enters as the nephew still wearing the beard.

Pip the potboy saves him by carrying the beard past the window on a broom. “There goes Uncle,” says Mr. Quince faintly. Mrs. Hobb has laid two dinners. She puts both on the bill.

volumes.title: The Goose Has the Whistle
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene: the parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green, where Mr. Quince the lodger owes three weeks and Duchess the goose goes where she likes.

Constable Dabney calls about a complaint of noise. He sets his whistle on the table, and Duchess picks it up in her beak and will not let go. After that every honk comes out as a shrill blast, and at every blast half the village runs in to see who is being arrested. The constable offers a reward. Mr. Quince chases the goose round the table, out of the window and back.

Mrs. Hobb holds out a crust. Duchess drops the whistle into her palm like a lady returning a glove. The reward goes to Mrs. Hobb. Mr. Quince asks whether it might come off his bill, and is told that it might not.

volumes.title: One Room, Twice Let
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act, in the parlour of the Sleeping Goose inn at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince owes Mrs. Hobb four weeks for the back room, and has had an idea.

He lets the room for the night to a traveller in buttons. An hour later he lets it again to a lady who lectures on thrift. There is one door. Mr. Quince spends the evening passing one guest out by the window as the other comes in by the passage, and serving the same cup of tea to each. At last they meet nose to nose in the doorway.

They are brother and sister, who quarrelled over a sideboard. They fall on each other’s necks, forgive everything, and go off arm in arm to her house without paying anybody. Mr. Quince sleeps in the parlour chair. Mrs. Hobb adds the chair to the bill.

volumes.title: The Wrong Trunk
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene is the parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince, the lodger, is five weeks behind with his board.

The carrier delivers a trunk marked with a large Q. Mr. Quince opens it and finds four dozen silver spoons. He concludes that a relation has died and done the decent thing. He orders supper for the whole village and promises Pip the potboy a pony. In the middle of the pudding a small furious man arrives. This is Mr. Quill, a traveller in cutlery, and he wants his samples.

Constable Dabney counts the spoons. One is missing. It is found in the nest of Duchess the goose, who gives it up with regret. The trunk leaves. The supper stays, on the bill, in Mrs. Hobb’s neatest hand. Pip is still asking about the pony as the curtain falls.

volumes.title: Soup for Seven
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act, set in the parlour of the Sleeping Goose inn at Mallow Green, where Mr. Quince the lodger owes six weeks.

Mrs. Hobb must go to her sister’s. She leaves Mr. Quince in charge for one evening, with a pot of soup for three and a week struck off his bill if nothing goes wrong. Seven members of a walking club arrive. Mr. Quince adds a jug of water for each extra guest and goes on stirring. By the time he ladles it out, the soup is clear enough to read through. He serves it as a broth in the Lowland style, celebrated for its lightness.

The walkers say they have never felt less weighed down. Mrs. Hobb returns to find them asking for the recipe. She strikes off the week. Then Mr. Quince, bowing, drops the tureen, and she writes it back on.

volumes.title: The Constable’s Trousers
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene: the parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince the lodger owes seven weeks, but tonight’s trouble, for once, belongs to someone else.

Constable Dabney has fallen into the duck pond while pursuing Duchess the goose on a point of law. His trousers are drying at the parlour fire, and he sits behind the table wrapped in the cloth. Enter the magistrate’s wife, come for tea. The constable cannot stand to greet her. Mr. Quince explains that the constable has taken a vow. Pip the potboy passes cups across so that nobody need move. All goes well until Duchess walks out of the door with the trousers.

The constable goes home after dark in Mrs. Hobb’s second-best curtain. Mr. Quince remarks four times that none of this was his doing. Mrs. Hobb agrees, and charges him nothing.

volumes.title: The Ghost on the Back Stairs
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act, in the parlour of the Sleeping Goose inn at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince, the lodger, owes eight weeks. Mrs. Hobb, it turns out, owes the brewery rather more.

Mr. Crimp, the brewer’s agent, comes to look the inn over with a view to taking it. Mr. Quince reasons that a new landlord would expect to be paid. So he wraps himself in a bedsheet and moans on the back stairs. Pip the potboy, who is fond of Mrs. Hobb, has had the same thought and the other sheet. The two ghosts meet on the landing, shriek, and fall into the parlour in a heap.

Mr. Crimp is delighted. A haunted inn, he says, is worth a third more, and he writes it in his book. He will be back. Mrs. Hobb looks at her two ghosts, then goes to iron the sheets.

volumes.title: The Inspector of Inns
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene is the parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green, where Mr. Quince the lodger is nine weeks in arrears.

Word comes that the county Inspector of Inns is travelling in disguise. That afternoon a pedlar of bootlaces walks in. Everybody knows at once. Mrs. Hobb brings the good plates. Constable Dabney salutes. Mr. Quince gives up his chair, waits at table with a napkin on his arm, and laughs at the pedlar’s only joke three times. The pedlar eats three dinners and is shown to the best bed.

Nobody has noticed the quiet woman in the corner, who had bread and cheese and fed her crusts to the goose. On her way out she leaves a card on the table. Mrs. Hobb reads it aloud: “Service uneven. Soup thin. Goose excellent company.” The pedlar is heard snoring overhead.

volumes.title: A Letter for Mr. Quince
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act, set in the parlour of the Sleeping Goose inn at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince has lodged in the back room ten weeks and paid for none of them.

The post brings him a letter, the first he has ever had here. The parlour decides it is a legacy. Mrs. Hobb pours him the good tea. Constable Dabney calls him sir. Mr. Quince will not open it; he says a sealed letter may hold anything, and an open one only what is in it. At last Pip the potboy reads it out.

A company of travelling players has seen the sample he sent. They will be in Mallow Green in two weeks and wish to see the rest. Nobody in the parlour knows what the rest might be. Mr. Quince takes the letter upstairs. Through the ceiling comes the sound of a pen.

volumes.title: Going, Going
volumes.text:
A comedy in one act. The scene: the parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green. Mr. Quince the lodger owes Mrs. Hobb eleven weeks, and Mrs. Hobb’s own debt to the brewery has come due.

Mr. Crimp, the brewer’s agent, holds an auction of the inn’s goods in the parlour. Up goes the table. Mr. Quince, who cannot bear to see it leave, bids. Up go the chairs, the good plates, the second-best curtain. He bids on each, against the constable, at one point against himself. Duchess the goose is put up, and he buys her too.

When the hammer stops, everything is still in the room and Mr. Quince owns all of it without a penny to his name. Mr. Crimp gives him until Saturday to produce the money. Mr. Quince sits down on his own table. Mrs. Hobb, for once, cannot think what to say.

volumes.title: The Bill Is Settled
volumes.text:
The last comedy, in one act. The parlour of the Sleeping Goose at Mallow Green, on Saturday. Mr. Quince the lodger owes Mrs. Hobb twelve weeks, and owes Mr. Crimp, the brewer’s agent, the price of every stick in the room.

Mr. Crimp arrives at noon. So does a wagon of travelling players. Mr. Quince comes down from the back room with a bundle of paper: eleven comedies in one act, each set in this parlour, with a landlady, a constable, a potboy and a goose. He has been writing down each week’s disasters. The players’ manager reads the first page standing, and laughs at the table. She buys the lot. It covers the brewery and the bill, with enough over for Pip’s pony.

Mrs. Hobb frames the receipt. Mr. Quince says the set wants a twelfth, sits down at the parlour table, and begins. Curtain.
